questions.question:
Choose the correct choice(s) regarding the following proportional logic assertion S:

[latex]S: (( P \wedge Q) \rightarrow R) \rightarrow (( P \wedge Q) \rightarrow (Q \rightarrow R))[/latex]

options.A: S  is neither a tautology nor a contradiction
options.D: The antecedent of S is logically equivalent to the consequent of S

questions.explanation:
Simplify the consequent: [latex](P\wedge Q)\rightarrow(Q\rightarrow R)\equiv(P\wedge Q\wedge Q)\rightarrow R\equiv(P\wedge Q)\rightarrow R[/latex], which is exactly the antecedent.

So S has the form [latex]A\rightarrow A[/latex], which is always true.

Answer: S is a tautology; its antecedent is equivalent to its consequent

questions.question:

Answer: 0

questions.question: An urn contains one red ball and one blue ball. At each step, a ball is picked uniformly at random from the urn, and this ball together with another ball of the same color is put back in the urn. The probability that there are equal number of red and blue balls after two steps is
questions.explanation:
Let the urn start with [latex]1[/latex] red and [latex]1[/latex] blue ball.

Step 1: A ball is picked uniformly (prob [latex]1/2[/latex] each). If red is picked, the urn becomes [latex](2R,1B)[/latex]; if blue is picked, the urn becomes [latex](1R,2B)[/latex]. Each case has probability [latex]1/2[/latex].

Step 2: We want the urn to end up with equal red and blue balls, i.e. [latex](2R,2B)[/latex] (since after 2 steps there are always [latex]4[/latex] balls total).
- From [latex](2R,1B)[/latex]: we need to pick the blue ball, probability [latex]=1/3[/latex].
- From [latex](1R,2B)[/latex]: we need to pick the red ball, probability [latex]=1/3[/latex].

So required probability [latex]=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{3}[/latex].

Answer: 1/3

questions.question:
The line graph L(G) of a simple graph G is defined as follows:
There is exactly one vertex v(e) in L(G) for each edge e in G.
For any two edges e and e' in G, L(G) has an edge between v(e) and v(e'), if and only if e and e' are incident with the same vertex in G.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
(P) The line graph of a cycle is a cycle.
(Q) The line graph of a clique is a clique.
(R) The line graph of a planar graph is planar.
(S) The line graph of a tree is a tree.
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- P: consecutive edges of a cycle share a vertex in a ring, so the line graph is again a cycle [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True
- Q: in [latex]K_4[/latex], edges 12 and 34 share no vertex, so the line graph is not complete [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] False
- R: the star [latex]K_{1,5}[/latex] is planar but its line graph is [latex]K_5[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] False
- S: line graph of [latex]K_{1,3}[/latex] is a triangle, not a tree [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] False

Answer: P only

questions.question:
The unit interval [latex](0, 1)[/latex] is divided at a point chosen uniformly distributed over [latex](0,1)[/latex] in [latex]\mathbb{R}[/latex] into two disjoint subintervals.

The expected length of the subinterval that contains 0.4 is ___________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Let [latex]U\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)[/latex] be the split point. If [latex]U>0.4[/latex], the sub-interval containing [latex]0.4[/latex] is [latex](0,U)[/latex], with length [latex]U[/latex]. If [latex]U<0.4[/latex], the sub-interval containing [latex]0.4[/latex] is [latex](U,1)[/latex], with length [latex]1-U[/latex].

[latex]E[\text{length}]=\displaystyle\int_0^{0.4}(1-u)\,du+\int_{0.4}^1u\,du[/latex]
[latex]=\Big[u-\tfrac{u^2}2\Big]_0^{0.4}+\Big[\tfrac{u^2}2\Big]_{0.4}^1=(0.4-0.08)+(0.5-0.08)=0.32+0.42=0.74[/latex]

Answer: 0.74

questions.question: A cycle on n vertices is isomorphic to its complement. The value of n is _____.
questions.explanation:
A cycle [latex]C_n[/latex] has n edges, its complement has [latex]\frac{n(n-1)}{2}-n[/latex] edges. Isomorphic graphs have equal edge counts:
[latex]n=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}-n\Rightarrow n=5[/latex]

Indeed the complement of [latex]C_5[/latex] (the pentagram) is again a 5-cycle.

Answer: 5

questions.question: Let [latex] G [/latex] be a directed graph and [latex] T [/latex] a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in [latex] G [/latex] that is rooted at a vertex [latex] v [/latex]. Suppose [latex] T [/latex] is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in [latex] G [/latex], rooted at [latex] v [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex] G [/latex] and tree [latex] T [/latex] ?

options.A: There are no back-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
options.B: There are no cross-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
options.C: There are no forward-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
options.D: The only edges in [latex] G [/latex] are the edges in [latex] T [/latex]

questions.explanation:
In a BFS tree, every edge [latex]u\rightarrow w[/latex] of G satisfies [latex]level(w)\le level(u)+1[/latex].

A forward edge goes from [latex]u[/latex] to a non-child descendant [latex]w[/latex], so [latex]level(w)\ge level(u)+2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] this contradicts BFS. Hence there are no forward edges [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

The others can fail:
- Back edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v}. Tree {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a} is both DFS and BFS tree; a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v is a back edge.
- Cross edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]b, b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a}. DFS visits a then b; b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a is a cross edge, and the tree is also the BFS tree.
- So G can also have edges outside T.

Answer: There are no forward-edges in G with respect to T

questions.question:
Consider a finite sequence of random values [latex]X=[x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}][/latex]. Let [latex]\mu _{x}[/latex]
 be the mean
and  [latex]\sigma _{x}[/latex]
 be the standard deviation of X .Let another finite sequence Y of equal
length be derived from this as [latex]y_{i}=a*x_{i}+b[/latex], where a and b are positive
constants. Let Let [latex]\mu _{y}[/latex]  be the mean and [latex]\sigma _{y}[/latex] be the standard deviation of this
sequence. Which one of the following statements is INCORRECT?

options.A:
Index position of mode of X in X is the same as the index position of mode of Y
in Y.
options.B:
Index position of median of X in X is the same as the index position of median
of Y in Y.

questions.explanation:
Adding b shifts every value; multiplying by a (positive) scales the spread.

- Mean: [latex]\mu_y=a\mu_x+b[/latex] (correct)
- Mode and median keep their positions (order is preserved)
- Standard deviation: [latex]\sigma_y=a\sigma_x[/latex], b does not appear [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] option 4 is INCORRECT

Answer: [latex]\sigma_y=a\sigma_x+b[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question:
Let N be the set of natural numbers. Consider the following sets.
P: Set of Rational numbers (positive and negative)
Q: Set of functions from {0, 1} to N
R: Set of functions from N to {0, 1}
S: Set of finite subsets of N.
Which of the sets above are countable?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- P (rationals): countable True
- Q (functions {0, 1} [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] N): pairs of natural numbers, N [latex]\times[/latex] N [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] countable True
- R (functions N [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] {0, 1}): infinite binary sequences, like subsets of N [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] uncountable False
- S (finite subsets of N): countable union of countable sets [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] countable True

Answer: P, Q and S only

questions.question: A bag has [latex]r[/latex] red balls and [latex]b[/latex] black balls. All balls are identical except for their colours. In a trial, a ball is randomly drawn from the bag, its colour is noted and the ball is placed back into the bag along with another ball of the same colour. Note that the number of balls in the bag will increase by one, after the trial. A sequence of four such trials is conducted. Which one of the following choices gives the probability of drawing a red ball in the fourth trial?
questions.explanation:
This is Polya's urn. By symmetry, every draw has the same chance of being red as the first draw.

Check for the 2nd draw: [latex]\frac{r}{r+b}\cdot\frac{r+1}{r+b+1}+\frac{b}{r+b}\cdot\frac{r}{r+b+1}=\frac{r(r+b+1)}{(r+b)(r+b+1)}=\frac{r}{r+b}[/latex]. The same holds for the 4th.

Answer: [latex]\frac{r}{r+b}[/latex]
